claim: Ribonucleotide reductases (RNRs) convert ribonucleotides into deoxyribonucleotides.
source: Ribonucleotide reductases (RNRs) convert ribonucleotides into deoxyribonucleotides, a reaction essential for DNA replication and repair.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about RNR function, supported by extensive prior research and stated as background knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The reaction catalyzed by RNRs is essential for DNA replication and repair.
source: Ribonucleotide reductases (RNRs) convert ribonucleotides into deoxyribonucleotides, a reaction essential for DNA replication and repair.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the biological role of RNRs.

claim: Human RNR requires two subunits for activity.
source: Human RNR requires two subunits for activity, the α subunit contains the active site, and the β subunit houses the radical cofactor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about human RNR structure and function, supported by prior research.

claim: The α subunit of human RNR contains the active site.
source: Human RNR requires two subunits for activity, the α subunit contains the active site, and the β subunit houses the radical cofactor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the functional organization of human RNR subunits.

claim: The β subunit of human RNR houses the radical cofactor.
source: Human RNR requires two subunits for activity, the α subunit contains the active site, and the β subunit houses the radical cofactor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the functional organization of human RNR subunits.

claim: A 3.3-Å resolution structure of a dATP-inhibited state of human RNR was determined by cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Here, we present a 3.3-Å resolution structure by cryo-electron microscopy (EM) of a dATP-inhibited state of human RNR.
evidence: This is the primary experimental result of the study, supported by the cryo-EM data collection and analysis described in the methods.

claim: The structure was determined in the presence of substrate CDP and allosteric regulators ATP and dATP.
source: This structure, which was determined in the presence of substrate CDP and allosteric regulators ATP and dATP, has three α2 units arranged in an α6 ring.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions under which the structure was obtained, as detailed in the methods section.

claim: The dATP-inhibited human RNR structure has three α2 units arranged in an α6 ring.
source: This structure, which was determined in the presence of substrate CDP and allosteric regulators ATP and dATP, has three α2 units arranged in an α6 ring.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The near-atomic resolution data provide insight into the molecular basis for CDP recognition by allosteric specificity effectors dATP/ATP.
source: At near-atomic resolution, these data provide insight into the molecular basis for CDP recognition by allosteric specificity effectors dATP/ATP.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data obtained in the study, specifically regarding the substrate-effector interactions visible in the structure.

claim: Lower-resolution EM structures of human α6 in the presence of both the anticancer drug clofarabine triphosphate and β2 were obtained.
source: Additionally, we present lower-resolution EM structures of human α6 in the presence of both the anticancer drug clofarabine triphosphate and β2.
evidence: This describes additional experimental structures obtained in the study.

claim: The structures support a model for RNR inhibition in which β2 is excluded from binding in a radical transfer competent position when α exists as a stable hexamer.
source: Together, these structures support a model for RNR inhibition in which β2 is excluded from binding in a radical transfer competent position when α exists as a stable hexamer.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the structural data obtained in the study.

claim: Drugs that target human RNR are used against some of the most aggressive and challenging to treat cancers.
source: Because RNR is vital for cell proliferation and genome maintenance, drugs that target human RNR are used against some of the most aggressive and challenging to treat cancers, including refractory lymphoblastic leukemia, metastatic ovarian and pancreatic cancers, and melanoma (Aye et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Drugs targeting human RNR are used against refractory lymphoblastic leukemia, metastatic ovarian and pancreatic cancers, and melanoma.
source: Because RNR is vital for cell proliferation and genome maintenance, drugs that target human RNR are used against some of the most aggressive and challenging to treat cancers, including refractory lymphoblastic leukemia, metastatic ovarian and pancreatic cancers, and melanoma (Aye et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Human RNR is a class Ia RNR.
source: Human RNR is a class Ia RNR, represented by eukaryotes and some prokaryotes that includes the well-studied homologs from Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cervisiae (Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2011; Brignole et al., 2012; Hofer et al., 2012; Minnihan et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Class Ia RNRs are represented by eukaryotes and some prokaryotes.
source: Human RNR is a class Ia RNR, represented by eukaryotes and some prokaryotes that includes the well-studied homologs from Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cervisiae (Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2011; Brignole et al., 2012; Hofer et al., 2012; Minnihan et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Class Ia RNRs include well-studied homologs from Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Human RNR is a class Ia RNR, represented by eukaryotes and some prokaryotes that includes the well-studied homologs from Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cervisiae (Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2011; Brignole et al., 2012; Hofer et al., 2012; Minnihan et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In class Ia RNRs, two homodimeric subunits work together to reduce diphosphate forms of all four canonical ribonucleotides to their deoxyribonucleotide counterparts.
source: In the class Ia RNRs two homodimeric subunits work together to reduce diphosphate forms of all four canonical ribonucleotides (NDPs) to their deoxyribonucleotide counterparts (Figure 1A–D) (von Döbeln and Reichard, 1976; Brignole et al., 2012; Hofer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about class Ia RNR function, supported by citations.

claim: The β subunit houses a stable diferric-tyrosyl radical cofactor generated by oxidation of a di-iron cofactor.
source: The smaller β subunit houses a stable diferric-tyrosyl radical cofactor generated by oxidation of a di-iron cofactor (Atkin et al., 1973; Sjöberg et al., 1978; Larsson and Sjöberg, 1986; Bollinger et al., 1991; Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2011) (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The α subunit contains the active site and two allosteric regulatory sites.
source: The larger α subunit contains the active site and two allosteric regulatory sites (Brown and Reichard, 1969b; von Döbeln and Reichard, 1976; Eriksson et al., 1997) (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Long-distance radical transfer from β2 to α2 generates a transient active site thiyl radical in α2 that catalyzes NDP reduction.
source: Long-distance radical transfer (RT) from β2 to α2 generates a transient active site thiyl radical in α2 that catalyzes NDP reduction and reverse radical transfer from α2 to β2 regenerates the tyrosyl-radical in β2 on every turnover (Licht et al., 1996; Minnihan et al., 2013b) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the RNR catalytic mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: Reverse radical transfer from α2 to β2 regenerates the tyrosyl-radical in β2 on every turnover.
source: Long-distance radical transfer (RT) from β2 to α2 generates a transient active site thiyl radical in α2 that catalyzes NDP reduction and reverse radical transfer from α2 to β2 regenerates the tyrosyl-radical in β2 on every turnover (Licht et al., 1996; Minnihan et al., 2013b) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the RNR catalytic mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: Inter-subunit radical transfer minimally requires formation of an α2β2 subunit complex.
source: This remarkable inter-subunit RT minimally requires formation of an α2β2 subunit complex (Brown and Reichard, 1969a; Rofougaran et al., 2006; Rofougaran et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Crystal structures of individual dimeric subunits from E. coli, yeast, mouse, and human RNRs have revealed general structural similarity.
source: Crystal structures of individual dimeric subunits from E. coli, yeast, mouse, and human RNRs have revealed general structural similarity (Nordlund et al., 1990; Uhlin and Eklund, 1994; Voegtli et al., 2001; Strand et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2009; Fairman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Eukaryotic α contains a conspicuous three-helix insert that is absent in E. coli.
source: Differences include a conspicuous three-helix insert in eukaroytic α (Xu et al., 2006) that is absent in E. coli (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: The C-terminal β2 tail interacts with a specific binding site on α2 and participates in inter-subunit radical transfer.
source: The unstructured C-terminal β2 tail interacts with a specific binding site on α2 and participates in inter-subunit RT.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the functional role of the β2 C-terminus.

claim: The α2 C-terminus emanates from a strand in the active site bearing two redox active residues on the radical transfer pathway (Tyr737 and Tyr738 in human α).
source: The α2 C-terminus emanates from a strand in the active site bearing two redox active residues on the RT pathway (Tyr737 and Tyr738 in human α, equivalent to Tyr730 and Tyr731 in E. coli α), which becomes disordered shortly following these Tyr residues, preventing direct observation of a pair of Cys residues that are required for shuttling reducing equivalents to the active site (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure and function of the α2 C-terminus.

claim: A pair of Cys residues in the α2 C-terminus are required for shuttling reducing equivalents to the active site.
source: The α2 C-terminus emanates from a strand in the active site bearing two redox active residues on the RT pathway (Tyr737 and Tyr738 in human α, equivalent to Tyr730 and Tyr731 in E. coli α), which becomes disordered shortly following these Tyr residues, preventing direct observation of a pair of Cys residues that are required for shuttling reducing equivalents to the active site (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the catalytic mechanism.

claim: RNR activity is regulated by a species-specific combination of allosteric, transcriptional, post-translational, and subcellular locational controls.
source: A species-specific combination of allosteric, transcriptional, post-translational, and subcellular locational controls regulates RNR activity to maintain appropriate concentrations and proportions of deoxyribonucleotides and ensures fidelity of DNA synthesis and repair (Hofer et al., 2012; Guarino et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Allosteric regulation of RNR depends on two nucleotide-binding sites in α2 that modulate α2 conformation and subunit oligomerization to tune activity and substrate specificity.
source: Allosteric regulation depends on two nucleotide-binding sites in α2 that, through modulation of α2 conformation and subunit oligomerization, tune activity and substrate specificity, as described below.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of allosteric regulation.

claim: The allosteric binding site that regulates substrate preference is located at the α-dimerization interface on one face of loop 2.
source: The allosteric binding site that regulates substrate preference is located at the α-dimerization interface on one face of a conserved structural element, called loop 2, whose opposite face makes contacts with the substrate base (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RNR structure and function.

claim: The opposite face of loop 2 makes contacts with the substrate base.
source: The allosteric binding site that regulates substrate preference is located at the α-dimerization interface on one face of a conserved structural element, called loop 2, whose opposite face makes contacts with the substrate base (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RNR structure and function.

claim: dATP binding to the specificity effector site results in a preference for CDP and UDP reduction.
source: dATP binding to this effector site results in a preference for CDP and UDP reduction; TTP for GDP reduction; and dGTP for ADP reduction (Brown and Reichard, 1969b; von Döbeln and Reichard, 1976) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about allosteric regulation, supported by citations.

claim: TTP binding to the specificity effector site results in a preference for GDP reduction.
source: dATP binding to this effector site results in a preference for CDP and UDP reduction; TTP for GDP reduction; and dGTP for ADP reduction (Brown and Reichard, 1969b; von Döbeln and Reichard, 1976) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about allosteric regulation, supported by citations.

claim: dGTP binding to the specificity effector site results in a preference for ADP reduction.
source: dATP binding to this effector site results in a preference for CDP and UDP reduction; TTP for GDP reduction; and dGTP for ADP reduction (Brown and Reichard, 1969b; von Döbeln and Reichard, 1976) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about allosteric regulation, supported by citations.

claim: Crystal structures of E. coli RNR with all four specificity effector-substrate pairs reveal the molecular basis of specificity regulation.
source: Recent crystal structures of E. coli RNR with all four specificity effector-substrate pairs (dATP-CDP, dATP-UDP, TTP-GDP, and dGTP-ADP) reveal the molecular basis of specificity regulation in this archetypal class Ia RNR (Zimanyi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: The rules of allosteric regulation of specificity appear to be conserved across RNRs.
source: Although the rules of allosteric regulation of specificity (Figure 1B) appear to be conserved, whether the molecular features of specificity regulation are the same in eukaryotic RNRs remains an open question (Xu et al., 2006; Ahmad et al., 2012; Zimanyi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on prior studies, with citations indicating ongoing debate.

claim: Whether the molecular features of specificity regulation are the same in eukaryotic RNRs remains an open question.
source: Although the rules of allosteric regulation of specificity (Figure 1B) appear to be conserved, whether the molecular features of specificity regulation are the same in eukaryotic RNRs remains an open question (Xu et al., 2006; Ahmad et al., 2012; Zimanyi et al., 2016).
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty in the field, supported by citations.

claim: For class Ia RNRs, dATP binding to the cone domain at the N-terminus of α2 has an inhibitory effect.
source: For class Ia RNRs, dATP binding to the cone domain at the N-terminus of α2 (Figure 1C,D) has an inhibitory effect, whereas ATP binding reverses this inhibition (Brown and Reichard, 1969b; Rofougaran et al., 2006; Rofougaran et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ATP binding to the cone domain reverses dATP inhibition.
source: For class Ia RNRs, dATP binding to the cone domain at the N-terminus of α2 (Figure 1C,D) has an inhibitory effect, whereas ATP binding reverses this inhibition (Brown and Reichard, 1969b; Rofougaran et al., 2006; Rofougaran et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In E. coli RNR, binding of dATP within the cone domain results in an α4β4 ring-shaped structure that holds the α2 and β2 subunits in a configuration incompatible with radical transfer.
source: In the prototypical system from E. coli, binding of the allosteric inhibitor dATP within the cone domain results in an α4β4 ring-shaped structure that holds the α2 and β2 subunits in a configuration incompatible with RT (Ando et al., 2011; Zimanyi et al., 2012) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies, supported by citations.

claim: ATP binding shifts the equilibrium from the inactive α4β4 state to the active α2β2 state in E. coli RNR.
source: ATP binding shifts the equilibrium from the inactive α4β4 state to the active α2β2 state (Rofougaran et al., 2008; Ando et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Activity regulation for E. coli RNR involves oligomeric state changes that are modulated by the ratio of dATP to ATP in the cell.
source: Thus, activity regulation for E. coli RNR involves oligomeric state changes that are modulated by the ratio of dATP to ATP in the cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data cited above.

claim: Eukaryotic RNRs do not appear to form α4β4-ring structures.
source: Eukaryotic RNRs do not appear to form α4β4-ring structures (Fairman et al., 2011; Aye et al., 2012; Ando et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Human α2 has the propensity to form α6 rings in the presence of both ATP and dATP.
source: Instead human α2 has the propensity to form α6 rings in the presence of both ATP and dATP (Rofougaran et al., 2006; Fairman et al., 2011; Ando et al., 2016) and the stability of the α6 ring appears to regulate activity (Ando et al., 2016) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: The stability of the α6 ring appears to regulate activity in human RNR.
source: Instead human α2 has the propensity to form α6 rings in the presence of both ATP and dATP (Rofougaran et al., 2006; Fairman et al., 2011; Ando et al., 2016) and the stability of the α6 ring appears to regulate activity (Ando et al., 2016) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Rings formed with dATP are stable, showing no oligomeric state change upon addition of β2.
source: Rings formed with dATP are stable, showing no oligomeric state change upon addition of β2, whereas α6 rings formed in the presence of ATP are unstable and disassemble into active state(s) upon addition of β2 (Ando et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: α6 rings formed in the presence of ATP are unstable and disassemble into active state(s) upon addition of β2.
source: Rings formed with dATP are stable, showing no oligomeric state change upon addition of β2, whereas α6 rings formed in the presence of ATP are unstable and disassemble into active state(s) upon addition of β2 (Ando et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Human RNR treated with clofarabine diphosphate or triphosphate leads to inactive enzyme and the formation of extremely stable 'persistent' α6 rings.
source: Support for the idea that 'stable' α6 rings correspond to an inhibited form of human RNR comes from studies with clofarabine (ClF), an adenosine analog used for cancer treatment, and related analogs cladrabine and fludarabine (Aye and Stubbe, 2011; Aye et al., 2012; Wisitpitthaya et al., 2016). In those studies, human RNR treated with CIF diphosphate (ClFDP) or triphosphate (ClFTP) lead to inactive enzyme and the formation of extremely stable 'persistent' α6 rings (Aye and Stubbe, 2011; Aye et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by citations.

claim: A 9-Å resolution crystal structure of human α was obtained in the presence of dATP.
source: Structural information about α6 rings has been limited to a 9-Å resolution crystal structure of human α obtained in the presence of dATP (Ando et al., 2016), a 6.6-Å resolution crystal structure of yeast α with dATP (Fairman et al., 2011), and a 28-Å resolution EM structure dATP-induced α6 from yeast in the presence of β2 (Fairman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: A 6.6-Å resolution crystal structure of yeast α with dATP was obtained.
source: Structural information about α6 rings has been limited to a 9-Å resolution crystal structure of human α obtained in the presence of dATP (Ando et al., 2016), a 6.6-Å resolution crystal structure of yeast α with dATP (Fairman et al., 2011), and a 28-Å resolution EM structure dATP-induced α6 from yeast in the presence of β2 (Fairman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: A 28-Å resolution EM structure of dATP-induced α6 from yeast in the presence of β2 was obtained.
source: Structural information about α6 rings has been limited to a 9-Å resolution crystal structure of human α obtained in the presence of dATP (Ando et al., 2016), a 6.6-Å resolution crystal structure of yeast α with dATP (Fairman et al., 2011), and a 28-Å resolution EM structure dATP-induced α6 from yeast in the presence of β2 (Fairman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Low-resolution structures of α6 rings were sufficient to establish the overall α6 subunit arrangement but failed to reveal the molecular basis for inactivity of the α6 ring.
source: These low-resolution structures were sufficient to establish the overall α6 subunit arrangement, but failed to reveal the molecular basis for inactivity of the α6 ring.
evidence: This is an assessment of prior structural work and its limitations.

claim: Human α forms ring-like particles composed of three α-dimers upon addition of 0.05 mM dATP.
source: Human α forms ring-like particles composed of three α-dimers (Figure 3A) upon addition of 0.05 mM dATP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D) as seen previously in the low-resolution crystal structures of human and yeast α (Fairman et al., 2011; Ando et al., 2016) and in human RNR in the presence of ClFDP (Aye et al., 2012) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study's negative stain EM data, consistent with prior structural studies.

claim: α6 rings formed with dATP alone showed some structural flexibility.
source: These α6 rings formed with dATP alone showed some structural flexibility.
evidence: This is an observation from the negative stain EM data in the current study.

claim: α6 rings were the predominant form observed following incubation of α with 1 mM ATP.
source: α6 rings were also the predominant form observed following incubation of α with 1 mM ATP, but some particles were incomplete or partially open rings, indicating that the subunit contacts are tenuous, consistent with the proposition that the rings formed in the presence of ATP are not stable (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the negative stain EM data in the current study.

claim: Some particles with 1 mM ATP were incomplete or partially open rings, indicating that the subunit contacts are tenuous.
source: α6 rings were also the predominant form observed following incubation of α with 1 mM ATP, but some particles were incomplete or partially open rings, indicating that the subunit contacts are tenuous, consistent with the proposition that the rings formed in the presence of ATP are not stable (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation from the negative stain EM data.

claim: Increasing ATP concentration to 3 mM resulted in an increase in the proportion of dissociated rings and free α-dimers.
source: Increasing ATP concentration to 3 mM resulted in an increase in the proportion of dissociated rings and free α-dimers.
evidence: This is an observation from the negative stain EM data in the current study.

claim: At 10 mM ATP, fewer α6 rings were observed and a filamentous form of α is apparent.
source: At 10 mM ATP we observed fewer α6 rings and a filamentous form of α is now apparent.
evidence: This is an observation from the negative stain EM data in the current study.

claim: The filamentous oligomers are composed of α2 units chained together end-to-end, often only three units in length.
source: Analysis of the filamentous oligomers showed that they are composed of α2 units chained together end-to-end, often only three units in length.
evidence: This is an observation from analysis of the negative stain EM data.

claim: With TTP, the dimeric α2 form is present exclusively.
source: With TTP, the dimeric α2 form is present exclusively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) as seen in prior studies (Thelander et al., 1980; Reichard et al., 2000; Rofougaran et al., 2006; Aye and Stubbe, 2011; Fairman et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an observation from the current study's negative stain EM data, consistent with prior studies.

claim: In dividing cells where RNR is actively producing deoxynucleotides, the dATP concentration is approximately 0.024 mM and the ATP concentration is approximately 3 mM.
source: In dividing cells where RNR is actively producing deoxynucleotides, the dATP concentration is approximately 0.024 mM and the ATP concentration is approximately 3 mM (Traut, 1994), thus the combination of 0.05 mM dATP and 3 mM ATP is expected to mimic cellular effector concentrations under which this higher dATP concentration inhibits RNR.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: The combination of 0.05 mM dATP and 3 mM ATP is expected to mimic cellular effector concentrations under which this higher dATP concentration inhibits RNR.
source: In dividing cells where RNR is actively producing deoxynucleotides, the dATP concentration is approximately 0.024 mM and the ATP concentration is approximately 3 mM (Traut, 1994), thus the combination of 0.05 mM dATP and 3 mM ATP is expected to mimic cellular effector concentrations under which this higher dATP concentration inhibits RNR.
evidence: This is an inference based on known cellular concentrations.

claim: 0.05 mM dATP inhibits human RNR even in the presence of 3 mM ATP.
source: To verify that 0.05 mM dATP inhibits human RNR even in the presence of 3 mM ATP, enzyme assays were performed, which showed inactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from enzyme activity assays performed in the current study.

claim: The combination of 0.05 mM dATP and 3 mM ATP yielded data sets in which α6 rings are preponderant and could be combined into a well-defined 3D structure with D3 point group symmetry.
source: Under negative stain EM, this combination of effectors (0.05 mM dATP and 3 mM ATP) yielded data sets in which α6 rings are preponderant and could be combined into a well-defined 3D structure with D3 point group symmetry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is an observation from the negative stain EM analysis in the current study.

claim: The combination of 0.05 mM dATP and 3 mM ATP provided the most structurally homogeneous preparation of α6 rings.
source: Given that this combination of effectors provided the most structurally homogeneous preparation of α6 rings, we used it for the high-resolution cryo-EM analysis.
evidence: This is an assessment based on the negative stain EM screening results.

claim: Structural stability of human RNR α6 rings is sensitive to nucleotide identity and concentration.
source: It is unfortunate that structural stability is so sensitive to nucleotide identity and concentration, since these constraints limit the ability to determine high-resolution structures of the human RNR with all combinations of substrate and effectors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations from the negative stain EM screening experiments.

claim: The near-atomic resolution structure was determined in the presence of substrate CDP and effectors dATP and ATP.
source: The near-atomic resolution structure described below was determined in the presence of substrate CDP and effectors dATP and ATP.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for the high-resolution cryo-EM structure.

claim: The cryo-EM structure has an overall resolution of approximately 3.3 Å.
source: The initial map was used as reference for refinement of image alignment parameters using SPARX, to obtain a final map that has an overall resolution of approximately 3.3 Å, and a maximum resolution of 3.15 Å around the α-α dimer interface (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a direct result from the cryo-EM data processing and resolution assessment.

claim: The cryo-EM structure has a maximum resolution of 3.15 Å around the α-α dimer interface.
source: The initial map was used as reference for refinement of image alignment parameters using SPARX, to obtain a final map that has an overall resolution of approximately 3.3 Å, and a maximum resolution of 3.15 Å around the α-α dimer interface (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a direct result from the cryo-EM data processing and local resolution assessment.

claim: At 3.3-Å resolution, densities can be distinguished clearly for the spiraling backbone of α-helices, the strands of β-sheets, residue side chains, and bound substrate and effector nucleotides.
source: At this resolution densities can be distinguished clearly for the spiraling backbone of α-helices, the strands of β-sheets, residue side chains, and bound substrate and effector nucleotides (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation about the quality of the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The final model contains six α subunits with residues 1 through 743 of the 792 amino acids.
source: The final model contains six α subunits with residues 1 through 743 of the 792 amino acids.
evidence: This describes the content of the final atomic model built into the cryo-EM density.

claim: dATP was the nucleotide included in the final model because it is a better fit to the density in both allosteric sites and is expected to have higher affinity for both sites.
source: Although both ATP and dATP were present, dATP was the nucleotide included in the final model, because it is a better fit to the density in both allosteric sites and is also expected to have higher affinity for both sites (Brown and Reichard, 1969b; Reichard et al., 2000; Kashlan and Cooperman, 2003).
evidence: This is a modeling decision based on density fit and prior knowledge about nucleotide binding affinities.

claim: Each α subunit in the final model contained one CDP in the active site, one dATP in the specificity site and one dATP in the activity site.
source: Thus, each α subunit contained one CDP in the active site, one dATP in the specificity site and one dATP in the activity site.
evidence: This describes the ligands modeled in the final structure.

claim: Six α subunits, organized as three dimeric units, make contacts through their cone domains to assemble an α6 ring.
source: Six α subunits, organized as three dimeric units, make contacts through their cone domains to assemble an α6 ring that resembles the overall arrangement seen previously in lower resolution crystal structures of dATP-inhibited human (Ando et al., 2016) and yeast α (Fairman et al., 2011) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The α6 ring resembles the overall arrangement seen previously in lower resolution crystal structures of dATP-inhibited human and yeast α.
source: Six α subunits, organized as three dimeric units, make contacts through their cone domains to assemble an α6 ring that resembles the overall arrangement seen previously in lower resolution crystal structures of dATP-inhibited human (Ando et al., 2016) and yeast α (Fairman et al., 2011) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current structure with prior structures, supported by citations.

claim: The α6 ring is ~180 Å in diameter and ~80 Å thick.
source: The α6 ring is ~180 Å in diameter and ~80 Å thick with a central hole that is constricted to 60 Å near each opening but widens to ~80 Å midway through the ring's interior.
evidence: This is a measurement from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The α6 ring has a central hole that is constricted to 60 Å near each opening but widens to ~80 Å midway through the ring's interior.
source: The α6 ring is ~180 Å in diameter and ~80 Å thick with a central hole that is constricted to 60 Å near each opening but widens to ~80 Å midway through the ring's interior.
evidence: This is a measurement from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Each α subunit from the α6 ring is similar to the 2.4-Å resolution crystal structure of human α2 with an RMSD over 738 Cα atoms of 2.25 Å.
source: Each α subunit from the α6 ring is similar to the 2.4-Å resolution crystal structure of human α2 (Fairman et al., 2011) with an RMSD over 738 Cα atoms of 2.25 Å.
